topic.title: The ten-minute kitchen
topic.claim: Quick-delivery apps are slowly teaching you to stop keeping things at home, so you pay a fee every time you run out.
topic.moment: You order one packet of curd and a lemon at 9 pm because the fridge is empty again.

turn.actually: It moves your pantry into their dark store, and you pay rent on it each time you order.

topic.feeling: I'm spending more and planning less, and I can't tell where it went.
topic.villain: Handling, small-cart and late-night fees on top-up orders
topic.because: If your home stays empty, you come back daily. Daily small orders pay better than one big monthly one.
topic.payoff: What happens next: a whole generation that has never stocked a kitchen, renting one by the minute.
topic.behaviour: People order single items several times a week instead of a monthly stock-up.
topic.mechanism: Frequent small orders carry fees that one large order wouldn't.
topic.send_to: The flatmate who orders onions three times a week
topic.why_now: Quick commerce now sells almost everything, so the empty kitchen feels normal.

score.why: The 9pm curd-and-lemon order is every flatmate's habit, and 'renting your pantry by the minute' is a turn they haven't seen.

notes: slides 6-7: the mechanism contradicts itself. Slide 6 says the app wants many small orders. But the small-cart fee exists because tiny orders cost the app money, and slide 7 shows the app pushing a bigger cart. Make it one idea: the app wants you back every few days AND wants each visit padded. Suggested direction: 'An empty kitchen brings you back every few days. The small-cart fee makes sure each visit is never small.' This also stops 'Your empty fridge is the business model' reading as a secret plan stated as fact, because the reader can see the fee doing the work at checkout.

slide 3: '75% of online grocery buyers say their unplanned buying has gone up. It's you.' The number is about impulse buying, not about stopping stocking up, so here it interrupts the curd-and-lemon scene. Move it to just after the chips on slide 7, where 'unplanned' is exactly what the reader just did. Keep the wording as close to the source as it is now. Drop 'It's you.' because it scolds; the chips already caught the reader.

slide 9: 'You carried the steel dabbas from home to this city. / They hold nothing.' leans wistful, and the close loses the cover's 'rent'. Keep the dark store line, cash in the rent image, and land the topic's payoff (a generation that never stocks a kitchen). For example: 'Your real kitchen is a dark store two streets away. You pay rent on it every time you run out.' Cut the dabbas, or keep them to half a line with no ache.

slide 2 or 5: the app is never named, and naming it is what makes the reader see their own phone. Add 'Blinkit, Zepto, Instamart' once, as texture, e.g. on slide 5: 'Then the checkout. Blinkit, Zepto, Instamart, same story.' Also add one detail beyond sight on slide 2: the doorbell nine minutes later, or the cold curd packet in your hand.

slides 6-7: two mirrored pairs read engineered: 'A monthly stock-up brings you to the app once. An empty kitchen brings you back every few days.' and 'The fee is gone. The bill is bigger.' Keep one and break the other's symmetry. For example: 'The fee disappears. The chips stay, and so does the bigger bill.' Also slide 8's 'It's not laziness' answers a charge the card never made. Open with the reason instead: 'The rent is ₹50,000, the kitchen is tiny, and the lease ends in eleven months.'

sources.fact: A 2022 LocalCircles survey found 1 in 4 online-grocery households used quick-commerce apps, only 1 in 10 placed over 10 orders a month, and most used them for last-minute essentials, which only partly backs the idea of frequent small orders.
sources.stance: neutral: the survey shows top-up use, mainly for last-minute essentials, but says nothing on whether apps cause people to stop stocking up or whether daily small orders pay platforms better.
sources.excerpt: 1 in 4 Indian households that shop for groceries online is using Quick Commerce apps. 1 in 10 households buying groceries online is placing over 10 orders a month via Quick Commerce apps. using them to purchase last minute essentials or indulgence foods

sources.fact: Datum Intelligence data reported in November 2024 shows 75% of online grocery buyers increased unplanned purchases, most spend over Rs 400 per order, and 46% cut spending at kirana shops.
sources.stance: neutral: it supports a shift towards impulse and frequent buying and away from kiranas, but it doesn't discuss platform economics or fees. Most buyers spending over Rs 400 per order suggests orders are not all tiny.
sources.excerpt: 75 per cent of online grocery buyers have increased their unplanned purchases in the past six months. with a majority of them spending over Rs 400 per order. Nearly half (46 per cent) of respondents report reduced spending at Kirana shops. over 82 per cent of consumers have shifted at least one-fourth of their grocery spending from Kirana stores

sources.fact: A LocalCircles survey reported in October 2026 found 69% of quick-commerce users typically spend Rs 200-999 per order and only 16% spend Rs 1,000 or more.
sources.stance: neutral: it gives order-size data only. It says nothing on order frequency or stocking up, and it suggests users now weigh value over speed.
sources.excerpt: Overall, 69% of users typically spend ₹200–₹999 per order, while only 16% spend ₹1,000 or more. they are paying more attention to what they get for their money than how quickly it arrives. many households are holding back purchases until closer to the festival amid economic uncertainty.

cover.headline: Ten-minute delivery taught you to [keep nothing at home].
cover.sub: And every time you run out, there's a fee.

paragraphs:
Ten-minute delivery taught you to keep nothing at home.
Swipe to read →
You've done this. Curd and one lemon at 9 pm, because the fridge is empty again. Again.
Nobody keeps a spare packet of Maggi anymore.
"Abhi mangwa lete hain" has replaced the monthly kirana list.
slides.why_swipe: So what does 'abhi mangwa lete hain' actually cost?

paragraphs: Then you hit checkout and there's a handling fee, a small-cart fee, and a late-night fee too.
Small enough to ignore. Three times a week, it isn't.
slides.why_swipe: Why would an app want you ordering so little, so often?

paragraphs: Those fees come with every order, not once a month. So one big monthly stock-up pays the handling fee once, and skips the small-cart fee.
Ten small top-ups pay them ten times.
slides.why_swipe: So where is your kitchen now?

paragraphs: The shelves at home stay empty. The stock sits in the app's warehouse down the road.
You still have a kitchen. You just pay rent every time you open it.

end.save: Read it again the next time you order one lemon at 9 pm.
end.send: Send to the flatmate who orders onions three times a week.

draft.alt_text: A six-slide text post arguing that ten-minute delivery apps have taught us to keep nothing at home, so we pay a fee every time we run out. Ordering curd and one lemon at 9 pm, no spare packet of Maggi, 'abhi mangwa lete hain' replacing the monthly kirana list, and the handling, small-cart and late-night fees at checkout. The fees come with every order, so one big monthly stock-up pays the handling fee once and skips the small-cart fee, while ten small top-ups pay them ten times. It ends with empty shelves at home, the stock sitting in the app's warehouse down the road, and the line that you still have a kitchen but pay rent every time you open it.
